problems.title: Maximal Network Rank
problems.description:
A country has `n` cities numbered `0..n-1` and a list of bidirectional `roads`, where `roads[i] = [a, b]` joins two different cities. No pair of cities is joined by more than one road.

The **network rank** of two distinct cities is the number of roads touching at least one of them. A road that touches both cities is counted only once.

Return the maximum network rank over all pairs of distinct cities.

examples.explanation: Cities 0 and 1 have degrees 2 and 3 and share one road: 2 + 3 - 1 = 4.

constraints: All pairs [a, b] are distinct as unordered pairs
problems.complexity: O(n^2 + r) time, O(n + r) space
hints: Count how many roads touch each city (its degree).
For a pair (i, j) the rank is degree[i] + degree[j], minus 1 if i and j are directly connected.
Store roads in a set of normalised pairs so the connected check is O(1), then try all pairs; n is only 500.

problems.title: Cheapest Cable Network
problems.description:
You are laying cable between `points[i] = [x, y]` on a plane. Connecting two points costs their **Manhattan distance**: `|x1 - x2| + |y1 - y2|`.

Return the minimum total cost so that every pair of points is connected, directly or through other points (the cables form a connected network).
problems.complexity: O(n^2) time, O(n) space (Prim on a dense graph)
hints: This is a minimum spanning tree over a complete graph.
Kruskal needs ~n^2/2 sorted edges. For a dense graph Prim without a heap is simpler and leaner.
Keep dist[v] = cheapest known edge from the tree to v; repeatedly add the unvisited vertex with the smallest dist and relax the others.

problems.title: Minimum Conference Rooms
problems.description:
Each meeting is a half-open interval `[start, end)`. A meeting that ends at time `t` frees its room for another meeting that starts at exactly `t`.

Given a list of `intervals`, return the minimum number of rooms needed so that no two overlapping meetings share a room. Return `0` for an empty list.

examples.explanation: [0,30) overlaps both other meetings, which do not overlap each other.

problems.complexity: O(n log n) time, O(n) space
hints: The answer is the largest number of meetings running at the same instant.
Sort the start times and the end times separately; you do not need to keep them paired.
Walk through the starts: if the earliest unfinished end is <= this start, a room is reused (advance the end pointer); otherwise open a new room.

problems.title: Count Message Decodings
problems.description:
A message of digits is encoded with `A = 1, B = 2, ..., Z = 26`. A digit string can usually be split into letters in several ways: `"226"` can be read as `2|2|6`, `22|6` or `2|26`.

A group such as `"06"` or `"0"` is **not** valid (no leading zeros, and `0` alone maps to nothing).

Return the number of different ways to decode the digit string `s`, modulo `1_000_000_007`. Return `0` if there is no valid decoding.

examples.explanation: Only 10 -> J is valid; 1|0 is not.

constraints: s consists of digits only and may start with 0
hints: Let dp[i] be the number of ways to decode the first i characters.
dp[i] gets dp[i-1] if s[i-1] is not '0', plus dp[i-2] if the two-digit number s[i-2..i-1] is between 10 and 26.
Only the last two values matter, so keep two variables, and apply the modulo at each step.

problems.title: K Closest to the Origin
problems.description:
Given a list of `points` and an integer `k`, return the `k` points closest to the origin `(0, 0)` by Euclidean distance.

To make the answer unique, return the points **ordered by squared distance ascending, then by `x` ascending, then by `y` ascending**. Duplicate points may appear in the input and each copy counts separately.
problems.complexity: O(n log k) time with a heap, O(k) space
hints: Compare squared distances; a square root is unnecessary and risks float error.
A max-heap of size k lets you drop the farthest candidate as you scan, giving O(n log k).
Once you have the k winners, sort them by (distance squared, x, y) to match the required output order.

problems.title: Longest Palindromic Substring
problems.description: Return the longest contiguous substring of `s` that reads the same forwards and backwards. If several have the maximum length, return the one that starts **leftmost** in `s`.

examples.explanation: "aba" is also valid but "bab" starts first.

constraints: s consists of lowercase and uppercase English letters and digits; comparison is case sensitive
hints: Every palindrome has a centre: either a character or the gap between two characters.
From each of the 2n - 1 centres expand outward while both sides match.
Only replace the best answer when you find a strictly longer one so the leftmost wins ties.

problems.title: Count Subarrays With Target Sum
problems.description: Given an integer array `nums` (which may contain negative numbers and zeros) and an integer `k`, return how many **contiguous** non-empty subarrays have a sum exactly equal to `k`.
hints: A sliding window fails because negative numbers break monotonicity.
A subarray (i, j] sums to k exactly when prefix[j] - prefix[i] = k.
Walk once, keep a hash map of how many times each prefix sum has occurred, and add map[prefix - k] to the answer. Seed the map with {0: 1}.

problems.title: Spreading Rot
problems.description:
A `grid` holds `0` (empty), `1` (fresh orange) or `2` (rotten orange). Every minute, each fresh orange that is 4-directionally adjacent to a rotten one becomes rotten.

Return the minimum number of minutes until no fresh orange remains. If it can never happen, return `-1`. If there are no fresh oranges to begin with, return `0`.
hints: All rotten oranges spread at the same time, so think multi-source BFS.
Start the queue with every rotten orange and count the fresh ones.
Process the queue level by level; each level is a minute. At the end, if fresh > 0 return -1.

problems.title: Asteroid Field Collisions
problems.description:
Asteroids move along a line, all at the same speed. In `asteroids`, the absolute value is the size and the sign is the direction: positive moves right, negative moves left.

When two asteroids meet, the smaller one explodes; if they have equal size both explode. Asteroids moving in the same direction never meet. Return the state of the field after all collisions, in left-to-right order.
hints: A collision only happens when a right-mover is immediately followed by a left-mover.
Keep a stack of survivors. For each incoming left-mover, fight it against the top of the stack while the top is a right-mover.
Handle three outcomes: top smaller (pop, keep fighting), equal (pop, incoming dies), top larger (incoming dies).

problems.title: Best Freelance Schedule
problems.description:
A freelancer can pick from `n` jobs. Job `i` runs during `[start_time[i], end_time[i]]` and pays `profit[i]`. Only one job can be done at a time, but a job that ends at time `t` does not conflict with one that starts at exactly `t`.

Return the maximum total profit the freelancer can earn.
problems.complexity: O(n log n) time, O(n) space
hints: Sort jobs by end time. Let best[i] be the best profit using the first i jobs.
For job i either skip it (best[i-1]) or take it: profit + best[j], where j = number of earlier jobs with end <= start of job i.
j can be found with binary search over the sorted end times (bisect_right).

solutions.python:
from bisect import bisect_right

def job_scheduling(start_time, end_time, profit):
    jobs = sorted(zip(end_time, start_time, profit))
    ends = []
    dp = [0]
    for e, s, p in jobs:
        i = bisect_right(ends, s)
        dp.append(max(dp[-1], dp[i] + p))
        ends.append(e)
    return dp[-1]

problems.title: Group the Ones on a Ring
problems.description:
You are given a binary array `data` that is treated as **circular**: the first and last elements are neighbours. In one swap you may exchange the values at any two positions.

Return the minimum number of swaps needed so that all the `1`s form one contiguous block on the ring. If there are no ones, return `0`.

examples.explanation: Swap the 1 at index 2 with the 0 at index 1: the ones now sit at indices 4, 0, 1, which are adjacent on the ring.

hints: If there are m ones, the final block occupies some window of length m on the ring.
Swaps cost the number of zeros currently inside that window, so you want the window with the most ones.
Slide a window of size m across the array concatenated with its first m - 1 elements; answer = m - max ones in a window.

problems.title: Rising Islands
problems.description:
An `m x n` map starts as all water. Each entry of `positions` turns one water cell `[row, col]` into land. Land cells joined 4-directionally form an island.

Return a list where element `i` is the number of islands **after** the first `i + 1` operations. If a position is already land, the operation changes nothing and the count stays the same.
hints: Re-running a flood fill after every operation is far too slow. Maintain the structure incrementally.
Union-Find over cell ids r * n + c. Adding land: count + 1, then union with each land neighbour; every successful union is count - 1.
Skip duplicates with a land-set check first, and use path compression (iterative is safest in Python).

problems.title: Shortest Path Through Walls
problems.description:
A `grid` contains `0` for open cells and `1` for walls. You start at the top-left cell and want to reach the bottom-right cell, moving one step up, down, left or right.

You may smash through at most `k` walls in total (smashing a wall means stepping onto that cell). Return the minimum number of steps needed, or `-1` if it is impossible. Both the start and target cells are open.

examples.explanation: Walk the open path in 6 steps.

problems.complexity: O(rows * cols * k) time and space
hints: Plain BFS on cells is not enough: the same cell can be worth visiting again with more smashes left.
BFS over states (row, col, smashes_left); the first time you pop the target is the minimum.
Prune: record the largest smashes_left seen for each cell and only enqueue a state if it improves that value.

problems.title: Two-Row Sliding Puzzle
problems.description:
A `2 x 3` board holds the tiles `1` to `5` and one empty slot `0`. In one move you slide a tile that is 4-directionally adjacent to the empty slot into it.

The puzzle is solved when the board reads `[[1,2,3],[4,5,0]]`. Return the minimum number of moves to solve the given `board`, or `-1` if it cannot be solved.

examples.explanation: This parity can never be reached.

problems.complexity: O(6!) states, each with at most 3 moves
hints: There are only 720 arrangements, so search the state space.
Flatten the board to a string and precompute which indices neighbour each index.
BFS from the start; moves are reversible so use a visited set. If the goal is never reached, return -1.

problems.title: Shortest Window Containing a Subsequence
problems.description:
Given strings `s` and `t`, find the shortest **contiguous** substring of `s` in which `t` appears as a **subsequence** (characters of `t` in order, not necessarily adjacent).

If several windows have the same minimum length, return the leftmost. If no such window exists, return the empty string.

examples.explanation: "bcde" is length 4 and starts first; "bdde" has the same length but starts later.

constraints: s and t contain lowercase English letters only
hints: A window must start with t[0] and end with t[-1]; this is different from the substring variant.
Let dp[j] be the largest start index of a window ending at the current position that matches t[0..j] as a subsequence.
For each character of s, update j from high to low so one character is never used for two positions of t; whenever dp[last] is set, compare window lengths (strictly smaller wins, leftmost on ties).

problems.title: Burst Balloons for Maximum Coins
problems.description:
You have balloons labelled with the numbers in `nums`. Bursting balloon `i` earns `left * nums[i] * right` coins, where `left` and `right` are the current neighbours of balloon `i`. A missing neighbour (past either end) counts as a balloon with value `1`.

Burst all the balloons in the best possible order and return the maximum total number of coins.
hints: Choosing the first balloon to burst splits the problem badly because neighbours change.
Flip the thinking: choose the LAST balloon k to burst in an interval (i, j). Then its neighbours are the fixed boundaries i and j.
dp[i][j] = max over k of dp[i][k] + a[i]*a[k]*a[j] + dp[k][j], with the array padded by 1 on both sides. Fill by increasing interval length.

tests.title: Google-style Online Assessment
tests.description: Two hard algorithmic problems plus tricky complexity, probability and Python-semantics questions in the style of large-company online assessments.

mcq.question: What is the time complexity of `f(n)`?
mcq.explanation: The outer loop doubles `i` until it reaches `n`: about log2(n) iterations. Each iteration runs the inner loop, which halves `j` from `n` down to 0: also about log2(n) steps. Total is (log n) * (log n) = O(log^2 n).

mcq.question: What does this program print?
mcq.code:
def f(a, b=[]):
    b.append(a)
    return b

print(f(1), f(2), f(3, []), f(4))
mcq.explanation: The default list is created once. `f(1)`, `f(2)` and `f(4)` all return the very same list object, and `print` only formats the arguments after all four calls have run, so three of the four slots show the final contents `[1, 2, 4]`. `f(3, [])` uses a fresh list.

mcq.question: This function should return the index of the first element `>= target` in a sorted list (or `len(a)` if none). For which input does it fail?
options: It returns an index one too large for every input
It raises IndexError on an empty list only
It is correct for all inputs
It loops forever when the answer lies in the upper half, e.g. a=[1,3], target=2
mcq.explanation: With `lo=0, hi=1`, `mid=0`, `a[0]=1 < 2` so `lo = mid` leaves `lo` at 0 and the loop never ends. The update must be `lo = mid + 1`. (Also, the search range should include `len(a)` as a valid answer.)

mcq.question: A dynamic array grows by a fixed 1000 extra slots whenever it is full, copying all elements into the new buffer. What is the total cost of n appends?
mcq.explanation: There are n/1000 reallocations and the k-th copies about 1000*k elements, so the total is about 1000 * (n/1000)^2 / 2 = Theta(n^2). Growing geometrically (e.g. doubling) is what gives amortized O(1) appends.

mcq.question: Which graph makes Dijkstra's algorithm (binary heap, no re-processing of settled nodes) return an incorrect shortest distance?
options: A graph with a negative-weight edge but no negative cycle
A graph with parallel edges between the same two nodes
mcq.explanation: Dijkstra assumes that once a node is settled its distance is final, which only holds for non-negative weights. A negative edge discovered later can improve a settled node. Zero weights, parallel edges and disconnected nodes are all handled correctly.

mcq.question: What does this print?
mcq.code: print(len({1, True, 1.0, 2}))
mcq.explanation: `1 == True == 1.0` and they hash equal, so they collapse into one element; `2` is the other. The set has 2 elements.

mcq.question: How many structurally distinct binary search trees can be built from the keys 1..5?
mcq.explanation: The count is the Catalan number C5 = (1/6) * C(10,5) = 252/6 = 42. (14 is C4 and 132 is C6.)

mcq.question: When reading a stream of unknown length, you keep one stored item and, on seeing the i-th item (1-indexed), replace it with probability p. Which p makes the final item uniformly random over all items seen?
options: 1/n where n is the final length
mcq.explanation: With p = 1/i the i-th item is kept with probability (1/i) * (i/(i+1)) * ... * ((n-1)/n) = 1/n for every i. The stream length is unknown, so p cannot depend on n.

mcq.question: What is the tightest amortized cost per operation of union-find with both union by rank and path compression?
mcq.explanation: Tarjan's bound: m operations cost O(m * alpha(n)) in total. That is amortized (an individual find can still take O(log n)), so 'O(1) worst case' is wrong.

mcq.question: A cache cluster picks a server with `hash(key) % N`. Going from N = 9 to N = 10 servers, roughly what fraction of keys end up on a different server (uniform hash)?
mcq.explanation: A key keeps its server only if `h % 9 == h % 10`. Over one period of 90 hash values that is true for exactly 9 of them (h = 0..8), i.e. 10%. So about 90% of keys move, which is why consistent hashing (about 1/(N+1) moves) is preferred.

mcq.question: What does this print?
mcq.code:
def f(x):
    c = 0
    while x:
        x &= x - 1
        c += 1
    return c

print(f(44), f(255), f(1 << 20))
mcq.explanation: `x &= x - 1` clears the lowest set bit each loop, so `f` returns the popcount: 44 = 0b101100 has 3 ones, 255 has 8, and `1 << 20` has 1.

mcq.question: Solve the recurrence T(n) = 2T(n/2) + n log n.
mcq.explanation: Each level of the recursion tree costs about n log(n/2^k), and summing over log n levels gives Theta(n log^2 n). The basic Master theorem does not cover it, but the extended case 2 for f(n) = n^(log_b a) * log^k n gives n log^(k+1) n.

mcq.question: What does this print?
mcq.code:
gen = (x * 2 for x in range(3))
print(list(gen), list(gen))
mcq.explanation: A generator expression is exhausted after the first `list(gen)`; the second call sees nothing and returns an empty list.

mcq.question: What does this print?
mcq.code:
fs = [lambda: i for i in range(3)]
print([f() for f in fs])
mcq.explanation: Closures capture the variable `i`, not its value. After the comprehension finishes `i` is 2 (the last value of `range(3)`; in Python 3 the comprehension variable is local to it but the lambdas share that cell).

mcq.question: You must report the approximate number of distinct user IDs in a stream of 10 billion events, using a few KB of memory and tolerating ~1% error. Which structure fits?
options: A hash set of all IDs
A Bloom filter with a counter of insertions
A sorted array with binary search
mcq.explanation: HyperLogLog estimates cardinality with ~1% standard error in a few KB. A hash set needs memory proportional to the distinct count; a Bloom filter answers membership, and counting insertions that it reports as new undercounts due to false positives.

mcq.question: A robot moves only right or down from the top-left to the bottom-right of a 5 x 5 grid of cells. How many different paths exist?
mcq.explanation: The robot makes 4 right and 4 down moves in some order: C(8,4) = 70.

tests.title: Amazon-style Online Assessment
tests.description: Two graph problems plus technical questions and engineering-judgment scenarios, mirroring the mixed format of large retail and cloud company assessments.

mcq.question: What does this print?
options: TypeError is raised and nothing is printed
([1, 9], [2]) is printed after a TypeError message
mcq.explanation: `t[0] += [9]` first extends the list in place (`__iadd__`), then tries to assign the result back to `t[0]`, which raises TypeError. The exception is swallowed by `except`, but the list was already mutated.

mcq.question: Table `emp(id, dept, salary)`. Which query returns, for every department, the employees earning the second-highest DISTINCT salary of that department, correctly handling ties at the top?
options: Rank rows with `ROW_NUMBER() OVER (PARTITION BY dept ORDER BY salary DESC)` and keep rank = 2
Rank rows with `DENSE_RANK() OVER (PARTITION BY dept ORDER BY salary DESC)` and keep rank = 2
Rank rows with `RANK() OVER (PARTITION BY dept ORDER BY salary DESC)` and keep rank = 2
`ORDER BY salary DESC LIMIT 1 OFFSET 1` without partitioning
mcq.explanation: `DENSE_RANK` gives tied rows the same rank and does not leave gaps, so rank 2 is the second distinct salary. `RANK` skips to 3 after a tie at the top; `ROW_NUMBER` would return one arbitrary row; the LIMIT/OFFSET query is global, not per department.

mcq.question: A consumer reads from an Amazon SQS Standard queue and charges a credit card for each message. Which design is REQUIRED for correctness?
options: Rely on exactly-once delivery from the queue
Increase the visibility timeout to zero
Process messages on a single thread only
Make the handler idempotent, e.g. using a deduplication key stored with the charge
mcq.explanation: Standard queues provide at-least-once delivery and best-effort ordering, so duplicates can arrive. The consumer must tolerate them (idempotency key). A single thread does not prevent redelivery.

mcq.question: What is the time complexity of building a binary heap from an unsorted array of n elements using the bottom-up `heapify` procedure?
mcq.explanation: Most nodes are near the leaves and sift down only a few levels: the sum over heights h of (n / 2^h) * h converges to O(n). Repeated insertion is the O(n log n) approach.

mcq.question: Two threads each run `counter++` one million times on a shared non-volatile, unsynchronized `long counter` that starts at 0. What can you conclude about the final value?
options: It is at most 2,000,000 and may be lower, because increments can be lost
mcq.explanation: `counter++` is read-modify-write. Interleavings can make both threads read the same value and write the same result, losing increments. The value never exceeds 2,000,000 but can be lower, and varies run to run.

mcq.question: Which combination gives O(1) average `get` and `put` for an LRU cache?
options: Hash map plus doubly linked list
Hash map plus singly linked list
Balanced BST keyed by access time
mcq.explanation: The map finds a node in O(1); the doubly linked list lets you unlink an arbitrary node and move it to the front in O(1) because it has a `prev` pointer. A singly linked list needs O(n) to find the predecessor.

mcq.question: In how many different ways (unordered combinations) can you make a total of 5 using coins of value 1, 2 and 5, with unlimited supply?
mcq.explanation: The combinations are {5}, {2,2,1}, {2,1,1,1} and {1,1,1,1,1}: four.

mcq.question: What does this print?
mcq.code:
words = ['bb', 'a', 'cc', 'd', 'aa']
print(sorted(words, key=len, reverse=True))
mcq.explanation: `sorted` is stable and `reverse=True` preserves the original order of equal elements (it does not simply reverse the result). Length-2 words keep input order: bb, cc, aa; then length-1 words: a, d.

mcq.question: A DynamoDB table stores orders with partition key `status` (values: PENDING, SHIPPED, DELIVERED) and sort key `orderId`. At high write volume writes are throttled even though provisioned capacity is far above the average load. What is the most likely cause and fix?
options: Too few sort keys; add a second sort key
Eventually consistent reads; switch to strongly consistent reads
A hot partition because only three partition-key values exist; use a high-cardinality key such as orderId and index status separately
Item size too small; pad items to 4 KB
mcq.explanation: Throughput is divided across partitions by partition-key hash. Three distinct values concentrate traffic on few partitions. Use a high-cardinality partition key and a GSI (or sparse index) for status queries.

mcq.question: It is 02:00 and your on-call dashboard shows a 5% error rate that started 30 minutes after your team's deploy. You are not yet sure the deploy is the cause. What is the BEST first action?
options: Keep digging through logs to find the root cause before touching anything
Wait until the morning when more engineers are online
Roll back the deploy to restore service, then investigate the root cause with the incident still recorded
Silence the alarm so it does not wake others
mcq.explanation: Customer impact comes first: a rollback is fast, low risk and reversible, and it gives you a clean comparison for root-cause analysis. Investigating while customers are failing, waiting, or hiding the alarm all prolong the impact.

mcq.question: A teammate's pull request passes all tests, but you notice a nested loop on a code path that handles about 10,000 items at peak. How do you act?
options: Measure or estimate the cost, share the evidence in the review, propose an alternative, and agree on a fix before merging
Approve it; passing tests is the bar
Rewrite their code yourself and push over their branch
Escalate to the manager without talking to the author
mcq.explanation: Dive deep with data, give actionable feedback in the review and keep ownership with the author. Approving ignores a known risk, silently rewriting undermines the teammate, and escalating first skips the direct conversation.

mcq.question: Three days before launch you discover an edge case in your design that can lose a small number of customer records. Fixing it properly needs 5 days. What should you do?
options: Ship on time and hope nobody hits the edge case
Quietly delay the launch without explanation
Ask a junior teammate to test whether it happens
Tell stakeholders immediately with the risk, the options (delay, reduced scope, mitigation or monitoring) and your recommendation
mcq.explanation: Raise the problem early with facts and options so the owners of the trade-off can decide. Data loss must not be shipped silently, and hiding the delay destroys trust.

mcq.question: A customer reports a failure that you cannot reproduce. Only one customer has reported it so far. What is the best approach?
options: Collect request IDs and logs, add targeted instrumentation, keep the customer informed, and look for similar signals in telemetry
Ask the customer to try again next week
Assume the customer made a mistake
mcq.explanation: Rare failures are often real. Use the customer's identifiers to trace the request, add observability if the evidence is missing, and communicate. Dismissing the report risks a larger hidden issue.

mcq.question: A post-incident review finds that an outage was triggered when an engineer ran a destructive command against the production database instead of staging. Which action item is MOST effective?
options: Remind everyone to be more careful and discipline the engineer
No action; it was a one-off human error
Add guardrails: separate credentials per environment, a confirmation or dry-run step for destructive actions, and least-privilege access by default
mcq.explanation: Good postmortems fix the system rather than blame the person: make the unsafe action hard to do by accident. Blanket bans stop legitimate work and discipline does not prevent the next error.

mcq.question: Your team needs a durable queue with at-least-once delivery, dead-letter handling and moderate throughput. Building your own would take about 3 weeks; a managed service meets all stated requirements. What do you do?
options: Build your own queue for full control
Postpone the feature until a perfect solution is available
Use a database table polled in a tight loop
Use the managed service, document its limits, and revisit only if requirements outgrow it
mcq.explanation: Choose the simple solution that meets requirements and spend engineering time on the customer-facing problem. Note the limits so the decision can be revisited with evidence.

mcq.question: In a design review you disagree with a senior engineer's proposal on a data model. You have a benchmark that shows a 10x slowdown at expected scale. What do you do?
options: Present the benchmark and your reasoning, listen to their constraints, and commit to the decision made even if it is not yours
Stay silent because they are more senior
Build your own version in secret
Block the review until they agree with you
mcq.explanation: Disagree with data and commit once a decision is made. Silence hides risk; secret work and blocking damage the team.

tests.title: Microsoft Coding Round
tests.description: Three string, stack and DP problems under a tight clock, with a short quiz on OS, SQL and language semantics.

mcq.question: Which of these is NOT one of the four necessary (Coffman) conditions for deadlock?
mcq.explanation: The four conditions are mutual exclusion, hold and wait, no preemption and circular wait. Scheduling policy is not among them.

mcq.question: What is the time complexity of inserting n strings of average length L into a trie, assuming a fixed alphabet size?
mcq.explanation: Each insertion walks or creates one node per character, so O(L) per string and O(n * L) in total, independent of how many strings are already stored.

mcq.question: What does this print?
mcq.code: console.log([1, 2, 3].map(parseInt));
mcq.explanation: `map` passes `(value, index, array)` and `parseInt(value, radix)` takes the index as the radix. `parseInt(2, 1)` is NaN (radix 1 is invalid) and `parseInt(3, 2)` is NaN (digit 3 is not valid in base 2).

mcq.question: What does this print?
mcq.code: console.log(typeof null, typeof undefined, typeof NaN, typeof []);
mcq.explanation: `typeof null` is the historical 'object', `typeof undefined` is 'undefined', NaN is a number, and arrays are objects.

mcq.question: Query: `SELECT c.name, COUNT(o.id) FROM customers c LEFT JOIN orders o ON o.customer_id = c.id WHERE o.status = 'PAID' GROUP BY c.name;`. The author wants every customer listed, with 0 if they have no paid orders. What is wrong?
options: The WHERE on `o.status` removes the NULL-extended rows, so customers without paid orders disappear; move the condition into the ON clause
Nothing; LEFT JOIN keeps all customers
mcq.explanation: After the LEFT JOIN, customers with no match have `o.status = NULL`, and `NULL = 'PAID'` is not true, so WHERE discards them. Putting the filter in `ON` applies it before the outer rows are preserved. (COUNT(*) would wrongly count 1 for them.)

mcq.question: In Floyd's cycle detection, `slow` advances 1 node and `fast` advances 3 nodes per iteration. What is true on a list that contains a cycle?
options: It still always meets, only faster
It might never meet, depending on the parity of the cycle length and the distance between the pointers
It meets exactly at the cycle's entry node
It meets after exactly one loop of the cycle
mcq.explanation: The gap changes by 2 modulo the cycle length L each iteration. If L is even and the gap is odd, the gap never becomes 0 mod L, so the pointers step over each other forever. With a difference of 1 (fast = 2) every gap is reachable.

mcq.question: A system uses 32-bit virtual addresses, 4 KB pages and a single-level page table with 4-byte entries per process. How large is each process's page table?
mcq.explanation: 4 KB pages use 12 offset bits, leaving 20 bits for the page number: 2^20 entries * 4 bytes = 4 MB.

mcq.question: A service must update its database and also publish an event to a message broker, and the two must not diverge if the process crashes between them. Which pattern solves this without a distributed transaction?

Write to the database, then publish inside a try/catch
Transactional outbox: write the event to an outbox table in the same DB transaction and relay it separately
Retry the whole request from the client
mcq.explanation: With an outbox, the business data and the event commit atomically in one local transaction; a relay publishes (at least once) from the outbox. Options 1 and 2 can lose or duplicate one side after a crash.

mcq.question: You roll a fair six-sided die repeatedly until a 6 appears. What is the expected number of rolls?
mcq.explanation: The number of trials to first success is geometric with p = 1/6, whose mean is 1/p = 6.

mcq.question: What is logged by the three callbacks, in order?

mcq.explanation: A modified merge sort or a Fenwick tree over compressed values counts inversions in O(n log n). The naive double loop is O(n^2).

mcq.question: Why is a single `visited` set insufficient to detect a cycle in a DIRECTED graph with DFS?
options: DFS cannot visit all nodes of a directed graph
A visited set uses too much memory
A node can be reached again through a different path (cross/forward edge) without forming a cycle; you need to know whether it is on the current recursion stack
mcq.explanation: In a DAG a node may be reachable by two different paths, so seeing a visited node does not prove a cycle. Use three states (unvisited, in progress, done) and report a cycle only when you meet an in-progress node.

mcq.question: Typeahead must return the top 5 completions for any typed prefix over 10 million phrases in under 10 ms. Which design fits best?
options: Scan all phrases and filter with `startswith` on every keystroke
A trie where each node stores precomputed top-5 completions (or a pointer to them), refreshed offline
A hash map from every full phrase to its score
mcq.explanation: Walking a trie costs O(length of prefix), and caching the top-k at each node makes the answer immediate. Scans and unindexed `LIKE '%..%'` queries are O(N).

mcq.question: For a social feed where some accounts have 50 million followers, which fan-out strategy is most appropriate?
options: Poll the database every second from each client
Hybrid: fan-out on write for normal accounts, fan-out on read (merge at request time) for very high-follower accounts
mcq.explanation: Pushing a celebrity post into 50M timelines is slow and wasteful, while pulling for everyone makes reads expensive. A hybrid keeps reads cheap for most users and avoids write storms.

mcq.question: A shuffle iterates `for i in 0..n-1: j = random(0, n-1); swap(a[i], a[j])`. What is wrong?
options: Nothing; it produces a uniform permutation
It is biased: it has n^n equally likely swap sequences, which cannot divide evenly over the n! permutations; use `j = random(i, n-1)` (Fisher-Yates)
It is correct only for even n
mcq.explanation: n^n is not a multiple of n! for n >= 3, so some permutations must be more likely than others. Fisher-Yates picks j from the not-yet-fixed suffix, giving n! equally likely sequences.

mcq.question: Which statement about reconstructing a general binary tree (values may repeat) is FALSE?
options: The inorder sequence alone, without null markers, is sufficient
Preorder with explicit null markers is sufficient

Postorder with explicit null markers is sufficient

mcq.question: A fixed-window rate limiter allows 100 requests per calendar minute. What is its weakness?
options: A client can send 100 requests at the very end of one window and 100 at the start of the next, producing 200 in a short interval
It always rejects the first request
mcq.explanation: Boundary bursts allow up to 2x the limit within a short span. A sliding window log/counter or token bucket smooths this.

mcq.question: What is the time complexity of Dijkstra's algorithm with a binary heap on a graph with V vertices and E edges?
mcq.explanation: Each edge relaxation can push an entry (O(log V)) and each vertex is popped once; with lazy deletion the bound is O((V + E) log V).

mcq.question: Two objects each hold a strong reference to the other and nothing else references them. Under automatic reference counting (ARC) what happens, and what is the usual fix?
options: They are freed immediately because their counts reach zero
They leak, since each keeps the other's count at 1; make one of the references weak or unowned
The runtime's cycle detector always frees them
They are freed only when the app exits
mcq.explanation: Reference counting cannot reclaim cycles: each count stays at 1. Breaking the cycle with a weak (or unowned) reference lets counts drop to zero. A tracing garbage collector would reclaim the pair, but ARC does not.

mcq.question: Five threads each need two locks to proceed (dining philosophers) and each takes its left lock first, then its right. Which change reliably removes the deadlock while keeping the structure otherwise?
options: Impose a global order on the locks and always acquire the lower-numbered one first
Add a sleep between acquiring the two locks
Release the first lock if the second is busy, but retry immediately in a tight loop with no back-off
mcq.explanation: A global lock ordering breaks the circular-wait condition. Sleeping only changes timing; the retry loop without back-off can livelock.

mcq.question: What are the average and worst-case time complexities of Quickselect (finding the k-th smallest element) with a random pivot?
options: O(n log n) average, O(n log n) worst case
O(log n) average, O(n) worst case
mcq.explanation: Each partition roughly halves the search space on average (n + n/2 + ... = O(n)), but consistently bad pivots degrade to O(n^2). Median-of-medians gives worst-case O(n).

mcq.question: A C program sums a large `int a[N][N]`. Version A loops `for i { for j { s += a[i][j]; } }`; version B loops `for j { for i { s += a[i][j]; } }`. Which statement is correct?
options: A is usually much faster because C stores rows contiguously and A walks memory sequentially (cache-friendly)
Both run equally fast; the sum is identical
B is faster because column access is vectorised
A is faster only when N is a power of two
mcq.explanation: C uses row-major layout. Version A has stride-1 access, so each cache line fetched is fully used; B jumps by a whole row every step and thrashes the cache and TLB for large N.

mcq.question: In two's complement arithmetic, which identity holds for every integer `x`?

mcq.question: A column `v` contains the values 1, NULL, 3, NULL, 3. What do `COUNT(*)`, `COUNT(v)` and `COUNT(DISTINCT v)` return?
mcq.explanation: `COUNT(*)` counts rows (5). `COUNT(v)` ignores NULLs (3). `COUNT(DISTINCT v)` ignores NULLs and duplicates (1 and 3, so 2).

mcq.question: A notes app lets users edit offline on several devices and merges later. It currently uses 'last write wins' based on device wall-clock timestamps. What is the main flaw?
options: Timestamps cannot be stored in a database
It cannot work offline at all
Clock skew can make an older edit win, and concurrent edits silently overwrite each other; use version vectors or a CRDT/operational transform to merge
mcq.explanation: Device clocks disagree and concurrent edits to the same field cannot be ordered by time. Causality tracking (version vectors) or mergeable data types preserves both edits.

mcq.question: This function should reverse a singly linked list in place. Which statement identifies the bug?

    prev = None
    cur = head
    while cur:
        cur.next = prev
        prev = cur
        cur = cur.next
    return prev
options: The loop condition should be `while cur.next:`
`cur.next = prev` destroys the link to the rest of the list before it is saved, so `cur = cur.next` just moves to `prev`
mcq.explanation: After `cur.next = prev`, `cur.next` is `prev`, so the following `cur = cur.next` steps backwards (to None on the first pass) and the rest of the list is lost. Save `nxt = cur.next` first, then relink, then `cur = nxt`.

mcq.question: What is the total time complexity of draining a Python list of n items with `while lst: lst.pop(0)`?
options: O(1) per call, so O(n) total
mcq.explanation: `pop(0)` shifts all remaining elements left, costing O(len). Summed over n pops that is O(n^2). Use `collections.deque.popleft()` (O(1)) or iterate with an index.

mcq.question: Several threads run `counts[key] = counts.get(key, 0) + 1` on a shared `dict` in CPython. What is true?
options: The GIL makes it atomic, so counts are always exact
The read and the write are separate bytecode steps; a thread switch between them can lose increments, so protect it with a lock
It raises RuntimeError on concurrent access
It is only unsafe on multi-core machines
mcq.explanation: Individual dict operations are atomic under the GIL, but the read-modify-write sequence is not. Another thread can run between `get` and the assignment. Use a `threading.Lock`, `collections.Counter` per thread then merge, or a queue.

mcq.question: A limit-order book keeps buy orders in a binary max-heap by price. Orders are frequently cancelled by id. A plain heap makes `cancel` O(n). Which approach keeps O(log n) amortized operations?
options: Mark cancelled ids in a set (lazy deletion) and discard them when they surface at the top
Re-sort the whole array after each cancel
Linear scan to find and delete the order
Store orders in an unsorted list
mcq.explanation: Lazy deletion keeps heap operations logarithmic: a tombstone set is O(1) and stale entries are skipped when popped. An indexed heap (id to position) is the other standard answer.

mcq.question: You must report the running median of a stream of prices after each tick. Which structure gives O(log n) per update and O(1) median reads?
options: A max-heap for the lower half and a min-heap for the upper half, kept balanced in size
A sorted array with binary-search insertion
A hash map from value to count
mcq.explanation: Keep sizes within 1 of each other; the median is the top of the larger heap or the average of both tops. A sorted array insert is O(n) because of shifting.

mcq.question: Table `px(ts, price)` has rows (1, 10), (2, 20), (3, 60). What are the three results of `AVG(price) OVER (ORDER BY ts ROWS BETWEEN 2 PRECEDING AND CURRENT ROW)`?

mcq.question: Merging k sorted lists with N total elements using a min-heap of size k has which time complexity?
mcq.explanation: Each of the N elements is pushed and popped once, and the heap holds at most k items, so each operation is O(log k).

print(Counter('abracadabra').most_common(2))

print(bisect.bisect_left(a, 2), bisect.bisect_right(a, 2))

mcq.question: A market-data process hands ticks from one producer thread to one consumer thread with minimal latency. Which structure is the best fit?
options: An unbounded linked queue guarded by one global mutex
A bounded single-producer single-consumer ring buffer using atomic sequence counters
A database table polled every 10 ms
A sorted map keyed by timestamp
mcq.explanation: A pre-allocated ring buffer avoids allocation and locks: producer and consumer each own one index, which is the idea behind low-latency disruptor-style queues.

mcq.question: Why do exchange market-data feeds commonly use UDP multicast with sequence numbers rather than one TCP connection per subscriber?
options: One packet stream reaches all subscribers with low latency, and sequence numbers let receivers detect gaps and request retransmission on a separate channel
mcq.explanation: Multicast avoids per-subscriber copies and head-of-line blocking. Reliability is rebuilt at the application level using sequence numbers and recovery channels.

mcq.question: Is the iteration order of a Python `set` of strings guaranteed to be the same between two separate runs of a program?
options: Yes, sets are ordered by insertion
No, string hashing is randomised per process (PYTHONHASHSEED), so order can differ between runs
mcq.explanation: Sets are unordered, and since Python 3.3 string hashes are salted per process. Only dicts guarantee insertion order (since 3.7).

mcq.question: In a language with signed 32-bit integers, `mid = (lo + hi) / 2` is used in a binary search over indices up to 2,000,000,000. What goes wrong and what is the fix?
options: `mid` is always rounded up, causing an infinite loop
`lo + hi` can exceed 2^31 - 1 and wrap negative; use `mid = lo + (hi - lo) / 2`
Integer division is not allowed on signed values
mcq.explanation: For lo = hi = 1.5 billion the sum overflows int32. `lo + (hi - lo)/2` never exceeds `hi`.

mcq.question: A cache sits in front of a price database. Comparing write-through and write-back caching, which statement is correct?
options: Write-back gives lower write latency but can lose acknowledged writes if the cache node crashes before flushing
mcq.explanation: Write-back acknowledges after updating only the cache and flushes later; a crash before the flush loses data. Write-through pays the database write latency but keeps the database current.

mcq.question: An account has balance 100. Two concurrent requests each run `SELECT balance` (READ COMMITTED), check `balance >= 100`, then `UPDATE ... SET balance = <old> - 100`. What can happen and what is the best fix?
options: Both can pass the check and the result is wrong (a lost update or overdraft); use an atomic conditional `UPDATE accounts SET balance = balance - 100 WHERE id = ? AND balance >= 100` and check the affected row count
Only one can ever succeed; the database serialises them automatically
The database throws a deadlock error every time
Nothing; READ COMMITTED prevents all anomalies
mcq.explanation: Check-then-act across separate statements is a race at READ COMMITTED. Moving the check into the UPDATE's WHERE clause makes it atomic. `SELECT ... FOR UPDATE` or SERIALIZABLE isolation are alternatives.

tests.title: Uber Backend Assessment

mcq.question: Finding the 10 nearest available drivers to a rider is slow with a B-tree index on `(lat, lng)`. Why does a geospatial index (geohash, quadtree or S2 cells) help?
options: A 1-D ordered index cannot answer 2-D proximity queries efficiently; spatial cells map nearby points to nearby keys so you scan only a few neighbouring cells
It removes the need to compute distances
mcq.explanation: A range on `lat` still scans a whole horizontal band. Space-partitioning keys let you query the rider's cell and its neighbours, then rank by true distance.

mcq.question: A mobile client times out calling `POST /rides` and automatically retries. Which design prevents creating two rides?
options: Make the client wait twice as long
Require an `Idempotency-Key` header and store the first result under that key so repeats return the same response
mcq.explanation: The server cannot tell whether the first attempt succeeded. An idempotency key lets the retry be safe. Rejecting retries or lengthening timeouts does not remove the ambiguity.

mcq.question: A client acquires a lease-based Redis lock with a 10 s TTL, then pauses for 15 s (GC pause) and writes to storage. Another client now holds the lock. Which mechanism protects the storage?
options: A fencing token: each lock grant returns an increasing number and the storage rejects writes carrying an older token
mcq.explanation: Time-based leases cannot protect against paused clients; only the resource can refuse stale holders, which a monotonically increasing fencing token enables.

mcq.question: Ride events for the same rider must be processed in order across a Kafka topic with 12 partitions. What should the producer do?
options: Use `riderId` as the message key so all events for a rider go to the same partition
Send each event to a random partition for balance
mcq.explanation: Kafka orders messages only within a partition. A deterministic key keeps a rider's events together. Random partitions or more partitions do not preserve order.

mcq.question: Table `trips(driver, fare)` has rows (A,10), (A,20), (B,5), (B,NULL), (C,NULL). What does `SELECT driver, AVG(fare) FROM trips GROUP BY driver HAVING AVG(fare) > 7 ORDER BY driver` return?
options: Three rows: A 15, B 5, C NULL
mcq.explanation: AVG ignores NULLs: A = 15, B = 5 (only one non-null value) and C = NULL. HAVING keeps only groups where the average is > 7; NULL comparisons are not true, so only A remains.

mcq.question: What happens when `f(3)` is called?
options: Deadlocks, because `threading.Lock` is not re-entrant and the recursive call tries to acquire it again in the same thread
mcq.explanation: A plain `Lock` can be held only once; the nested `with lock:` blocks forever waiting for itself. Use `threading.RLock` or restructure so the lock is taken once.

mcq.question: Why do consistent-hash rings give each physical node many virtual nodes?
options: To spread load more evenly and to spread a failed node's keys across many survivors instead of dumping them on one neighbour
mcq.explanation: With one point per node the arc sizes vary widely and a failure shifts all its load to a single successor. Many virtual points smooth both effects.

mcq.question: During a network partition a CP (consistent, partition-tolerant) datastore with a 5-node quorum is split 3 / 2. What happens on the 2-node side?
options: It keeps accepting writes and merges them later
It refuses writes (and possibly reads), because it cannot reach a quorum
mcq.explanation: A CP system sacrifices availability on the minority side to avoid divergence. Accepting writes on both sides is the AP trade-off.

mcq.question: In the grid problem where you may smash up to k walls, how many distinct search states can BFS visit in the worst case for an R x C grid?
mcq.explanation: A state is (row, col, walls smashed so far), so there are R * C * (k + 1) states. Dropping the third coordinate gives wrong answers because the same cell can be worth revisiting with more smashes remaining.

mcq.question: 1,000 clients fail a call to a service and retry after exactly 1, 2, 4, 8 seconds (exponential back-off, no randomness). What problem remains?
options: The clients stay synchronised and hit the service in waves (thundering herd); add random jitter to each delay
Exponential back-off is not allowed in HTTP
mcq.explanation: Identical schedules produce synchronised bursts. Jitter spreads the retries over time.

mcq.question: An API gateway forwards a request to an upstream service that does not answer before the gateway's timeout. Which HTTP status should the gateway return?
mcq.explanation: 504 means the gateway did not receive a timely response from the upstream. 502 is for an invalid response; 503 means the service itself is overloaded or down.

mcq.question: Query: `SELECT * FROM trips WHERE city = ? AND status = ? ORDER BY created_at DESC LIMIT 20`. Which composite index serves it best?
mcq.explanation: Equality columns come first, then the ordering column: `(city, status, created_at)` finds the first matching entries and reads them in order, stopping after 20 rows with no sort.

mcq.question: A replicated store uses N = 3 replicas. Which read/write quorum sizes guarantee that every read sees the latest acknowledged write?
mcq.explanation: The read and write sets must overlap: R + W > N. 2 + 2 = 4 > 3 holds, while 1+2 = 3 and 2+1 = 3 do not.

tests.title: Lemon.io Senior Screen
tests.description: Senior-engineer judgement questions about architecture, migrations, incidents and trade-offs, plus one hard scheduling problem.

mcq.question: A six-person team is starting a new product whose domain boundaries are still unclear. Which architecture is the most sensible starting point?
options: Twenty microservices, one per guessed domain
A modular monolith with clear internal module boundaries that can be split later
One giant shared database accessed directly by all future services
mcq.explanation: Early boundaries are guesses; microservices make wrong guesses expensive (network calls, deployments, distributed transactions). A modular monolith keeps change cheap and preserves the option to extract services.

mcq.question: You must rename a heavily used column with zero downtime while several app versions run at once. Which sequence is safest?
options: `ALTER TABLE ... RENAME COLUMN` during the deploy
Take the app offline for the migration
Expand/contract: add the new column, dual-write, backfill, switch reads, then drop the old column in a later release
Create a new database and copy everything
mcq.explanation: A direct rename breaks old app versions instantly. Expand/contract keeps both schemas valid across deploys and allows rollback at each step.

mcq.question: Users edit their own profile through a form; two edits to the same profile at the same time are rare but must not silently overwrite each other. Which concurrency control fits?
options: Optimistic locking with a version column checked in the UPDATE's WHERE clause
Pessimistic row locks held while the form is open
Serialise all requests through one global lock
mcq.explanation: Conflicts are rare, so check-on-write is cheap: `UPDATE ... WHERE id = ? AND version = ?` and ask the user to retry/merge if no row matched. Holding locks while a human types is a bad idea.

options: Request coalescing (single-flight / lock per key), serving stale data while one worker refreshes, plus randomised TTLs
mcq.explanation: Make only one request recompute the value and let others wait or use stale data; jittered TTLs avoid synchronised expiry of many keys.

mcq.explanation: OFFSET must read and discard all skipped rows. Keyset pagination seeks directly to the position using the index and stays fast at any depth.

mcq.question: This ORM code lists 200 orders and prints each customer's name. Roughly how many SQL queries run (lazy loading)?
mcq.explanation: One query for the orders plus one lazy query per order for its customer: the N+1 problem. Fix with a join or eager loading (`select_related`/`include`).

mcq.question: A production API key was accidentally pushed to a public repository 10 minutes ago. What is the correct FIRST action?
options: Force-push to remove the commit and consider it handled
Revoke/rotate the key immediately, then clean history and audit usage
Wait to see whether anyone uses it
Make the repository private and continue using the key
mcq.explanation: Assume the key is compromised: automated scrapers harvest public pushes within seconds. Rotation is the only reliable fix; history rewriting is a secondary cleanup.

mcq.question: A test fails about 2% of the time because it asserts on `datetime.now()` near a minute boundary. What is the best fix?
options: Retry the test up to 3 times
Inject a controllable clock (or freeze time) so the code under test does not depend on real time
mcq.explanation: Flakiness from hidden inputs is solved by controlling the inputs. Retries and sleeps only hide the problem.

mcq.question: Users report a p99 latency spike on an endpoint that calls 12 internal services. Which tool should you reach for first to localise the slow component?
options: Distributed tracing, to see the span timings of a slow request across services
Aggregate CPU graphs of each host
A load test on the database
mcq.explanation: Tracing shows where time was spent for specific slow requests across service boundaries. CPU graphs and error logs lack the per-request breakdown.

mcq.question: After a user updates their name, the next page load (served from a read replica) sometimes shows the old name. What is the standard remedy?
options: Make replicas synchronous for all queries, accepting higher write latency everywhere
Provide read-your-writes: route that user's reads to the primary (or wait for the replica position) for a short window after a write
mcq.explanation: Asynchronous replication has lag. Session-level read-your-writes routing fixes the visible anomaly without removing the replica's scaling benefit.

mcq.question: You are shipping a risky change to the payment flow. Which rollout is safest?
options: Progressive rollout (1%, 10%, 50%, 100%) behind a feature flag with monitoring, alerts and a kill switch

Deploy to staging only and trust it
Ask customers to opt in by email
mcq.explanation: Limit blast radius, watch real traffic and keep a fast off-switch. Staging cannot reproduce production data and load patterns.

mcq.explanation: Removing a field is a breaking change for clients you cannot update. Version or deprecate with telemetry-driven removal.
